tagline.text: A museum of Ilocano life in a Spanish-era tobacco warehouse

location.label: Location
location.text: V. Llanes Street (corner of Gen. A. Luna Street, next to City Hall), Laoag City, Ilocos Norte

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱50–500 (admission plus local transport and snacks)

children.text: Museo Ilocos Norte (Gameng Museum) is a museum next to Laoag City Hall, in a Spanish-era tobacco warehouse built in 1878 and restored. With displays of Ilocano farming, the sea, the highlands, markets and village life, plus a replica of a traditional stone house, it is a good starting point for a trip through Ilocos Norte.

Museo Ilocos Norte is a provincial museum in Laoag City, the capital of Ilocos Norte. Its nickname "Gameng" is an Iloco word meaning treasure, and it is described as run by the Gameng Foundation. The building is the restored Camarin de Tabaco de la Tabacalera, a Spanish-era tobacco storage warehouse built in 1878. The museum's symbol is a many-rayed sun taken from a finial at the back of a 19th-century church in San Nicolas. It is described as built to instill pride in Ilocanos and is one of the few Laoag attractions often visited by students and tourists. It stands next to City Hall, a block from the city plaza, so it is within walking distance of Laoag Cathedral and the Sinking Bell Tower.

The museum is said to have opened on December 31, 1999, under Governor Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., replacing the Ilocandia Museum of Traditional Culture, which dated to 1977. According to a travel blog (March 2016), the displays are divided into 15 main sections organized by themes such as the Land, the Sea, the Highland, the Farm, the Market and the Town. English labels are provided throughout, and an English brochure comes with the ticket.

The most eye-catching exhibit is a replica of a two-storey bahay na bato (stone house). At the south end of the museum, it is modeled on the Lazo Residence in Bacarra and is fully furnished. The West Gallery has a dap-ayan (a village meeting place) and a pugon (a tobacco-curing furnace), and you can also see traditional clothing, weapons, household items, calesas and an alang (an Itneg house) from the ethnic groups of Northern Luzon. There are musical instruments such as the pito and ludag, a small theater showing a 15-minute video on musical traditions, and a room dedicated to the late President Marcos. Outside stands a dapil, a sugar mill.

The same complex has the Taoid museum, which presents Cordilleran culture, so the two are good to visit together. A 2016 blog describes both museums as in one complex on V. Llanes Street and says the Museo Ilocos Norte building is not air-conditioned but manageable with fans. This guide is for travelers spending half a day in Laoag; opening hours and fees differ by source, so it is best to check before you go.
The building itself is an exhibit. It is a restored Spanish-era tobacco storage warehouse, and its brick architecture is part of the display. In one corner, a
75 cm
-deep excavation made by the National Museum in February 2004 exposes the building's different floor levels.

A two-storey replica of a stone house modeled on the Lazo Residence in Bacarra. The dining room, kitchen and sleeping quarters are recreated with furniture, showing at a glance how a wealthy Ilocano household lived. It is described as the museum's most popular exhibit.

blocks.title: Land, sea, highland, farm, market and town

children.text: Ilocano life is presented through the themes of the land, the sea, the highland, the farm, the market and the town. The exhibits run from farming and tobacco processing to traditional clothing and recent history, and one reviewer recommends touring them clockwise.

The "dap-ayan" in the West Gallery is an open meeting place where villagers gathered, and the "pugon" is a furnace for curing tobacco. It is a place to understand in physical form why Ilocos is known as a tobacco region.
Traditional instruments such as the pito and ludag are on display, and a small theater introduces Ilocos Norte's musical traditions in a video of about
15 minutes
Outside the building stands the "dapil," a sugar mill. Together with the tobacco furnace inside, it is an exhibit on Ilocos agriculture.
A shop near the exit sells local food products, handicrafts and travel guides. It is a convenient place to buy Ilocos specialties as souvenirs.

Next door, Taoid is a two-storey museum that opened on November 17, 2015, and introduces the cultures of the Cordillera peoples and their relationship with the lowland Ilocanos. One blogger rated Taoid the more interesting of the two.

items.title: A half day at the museums
items.subtitle: Museo Ilocos Norte and Taoid

children.text: Walk from your hotel in central Laoag to the museum. Check the opening time before you go.
Buy your ticket, pick up the English brochure and tour the exhibits clockwise.
Take your time with the bahay na bato replica and the dap-ayan and pugon displays.
Watch the music video in the small theater and browse the gift shop.
Have lunch at a cafe or restaurant in the same complex, then move on to the Taoid museum.
See the Cordillera exhibits at Taoid and finish there.
Since the museum is next to City Hall, you can also see Laoag Cathedral and the bell tower in the morning and visit the museum in the afternoon.

items.title: A full day in downtown Laoag
items.subtitle: Cathedral, bell tower and museum

children.text: See Laoag Cathedral and the bell tower.
Move on to the museum and spend one to two hours looking around.
Have lunch with Ilocano food at a downtown restaurant.
Visit the Taoid museum.
Stroll through Aurora Park or the market to finish.
If you have another day, continue to Paoay Church and the La Paz Sand Dunes.
There are flights from Manila to Laoag International Airport (LAO). Airlines and schedules change by season, so check when you book.
From the airport, go into the city by tricycle or taxi. Check the fare locally.
Routes change often, so check airline announcements before departure.

According to Wikivoyage, buses from Manila (Cubao, Sampaloc and Pasay) to Laoag are run by companies such as Fariñas (F.R. Castro Street), GV Florida (Laoag-Paoay Road), Partas (Paco Roman Street) and Maria de Leon (A.G. Tupaz Street).
The trip takes about
10–12 hours
. Fares vary by company and seat class, so check locally.
Laoag has jeepneys, tricycles, calesas (horse-drawn carriages) and taxis. The museum is next to City Hall, a block from the city plaza, so you can walk to and from a hotel downtown.
The address is 33-C V. Llanes Street (per Wikivoyage), and it is also given as the corner of Gen. A. Luna Street and Don Vicente Llanes Avenue.

The museum is an indoor visit, so weather matters less, but Laoag has a tropical savanna climate and the dry season (November–April) is best for walking. According to the Wikipedia climate table, the wettest month is August (about 594 mm) and the hottest months are April and May (mean daily maximum about

The museum has been described as fan-cooled without air conditioning, so it can be hot at midday. In the hot season, visit early in the morning. About four to five typhoons a year are said to pass through, so in the rainy season the museum makes a good rainy-day alternative.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: Visit early in the morning; spend midday indoors

items.note: Some Wikivoyage listings were updated in 2015; check locally

children.text: Prices are approximate as of
and may vary with local conditions.

Laoag has lodging from budget places to five-star resorts. Wikivoyage lists budget places such as Texicano Hotel (₱350–470) and Star Light Lodge (₱270–550), and Ilocos Rosewell Hotel (from ₱1,200), Java Hotel (from ₱1,980) and Plaza Del Norte Hotel (from ₱2,500). These prices come from an old list, so confirm them when you book. To see the museum on foot, it is best to stay downtown.

For food, La Tabacalera Food Park is on the same street, and the museum complex is said to have cafes and restaurants. Dap-ayan ni Lawiswis, open from 5 AM to 1 PM, is recommended for the Laoag empanada. Hours can change, so check.
Opening hours differ by source (Monday–Saturday 8:00–17:00 with Sunday closed, or 9:00–17:00), so check with the museum (phone 077-770-4587) or the tourism office before you go.
One reviewer says touring the exhibits clockwise makes the flow easier to follow.
An English brochure comes with the ticket, so do not lose it.
There are reports that the building is not air-conditioned, so bring a towel for sweat and water.
Allow two to three hours if you also want to see Taoid. Ask locally whether there is a combined ticket for the two.
Buying souvenirs at the shop near the exit lets you pick out Ilocos specialties in one place.
The Taoid museum is said to let you touch some of its artifacts, but check the signs and follow staff instructions.
The Laoag City tourism office (phone +63 998 555 4080, email tourism@laoagcity.gov.ph) can give you up-to-date information.
Laoag Cathedral and the bell tower are close by, so it is easy to see them on foot on the same day.
Opening hours and closing days are hard to pin down because sources differ. Some say the museum is closed on Sundays and others say it opens on Sundays, so be sure to check before you visit.
Fees follow the Ilocos Norte tourism office information (2026 page); the ₱20 in an older blog appears to be an old fee.
The exhibit layout (15 sections, the location of the replica and so on) is based on a 2016 blog and may have changed.
The museum's official website address sometimes does not open, so use the phone or the tourism office for current information.
An old post says the museum closes while staff take lunch, so avoid visiting around noon.
Watch out for motorcycles and tricycles when crossing roads.
An Italian Renaissance-style cathedral and a sinking brick bell tower within walking distance of the museum. It is the city's first sight.
The capital of Ilocos Norte, where the museum is located. In
Laoag
you can find lodging, restaurants and airport transport all in one place.
A UNESCO World Heritage church on the road running south from Laoag. The buttresses of
Paoay Church
are a leading example of Earthquake Baroque.
Sand dunes on the coast northwest of Laoag, known for 4x4 tours and sandboarding. The
La Paz Sand Dunes
are close to the city.
